'''''Pelargonium peltatum''''' is a scrambling [[purple]]
[[perennial plant]] with five shallow or deeply lobed, circular- to heart-shaped, somewhat fleshy leaves, sometimes with a differently coloured semicircular band, that has been assigned to the [[Geraniaceae|cranesbill family]]. It carries umbel-like inflorescences with 2–10, white to mauve, [[Petal#Variations|bilateral symmetrical]] flowers, each with a "spur" that is merged with the flower stalk. It is known by several common names including '''ivy-leaved pelargonium''' and '''cascading geranium'''.<ref name=PZA>{{cite web|website= SANBI PlantZAfrica|title= Pelargonium peltatum (L) L'Hér..|url= http://pza.sanbi.org/pelargonium-peltatum}}</ref> It is native to the [[Cape Provinces]] of [[South Africa]].<ref name = powo>[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:376728-1 ''Pelargonium peltatum'' (L.) L'Hér.] ''[[Plants of the World Online]]''. Retrieved 29 September 2023.</ref> In its home range, it flowers year round but most vigorously from August to October.<ref name=CABI>{{cite web|website= Invasive Species Compendium|title= Pelargonium peltatum (ivy geranium)|url= https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/120128}}</ref>

== Description ==
The ivy-leaved pelargonium is a [[perennial plant]] that scrambles over the surrounding vegetation and its somewhat [[succulent]], slender and smooth, 3–10 mm (0.12–0.40 in) thick stems can grow to a length of about 2 m (7 ft). 

The leaves are [[Leaf#Arrangement on the stem|alternately]] arranged along the stem, but sometimes seem to be opposite. The leaves have broad oval to triangular [[stipule]]s of about 7 mm (0.28 in) long and 4 mm (0.16 in) wide, a [[Petiole (botany)|leaf stalk]] of ½–5½ cm (0.2–2.2 in) long, and a hairy or hairless, green to greyish green, sometimes with a differently colored semicircular band, more of less fleshy, circular to heart-shaped in outline, on average 3 cm (1.2 in) long and 5 cm (2.0 in) wide (full range 1–6¾ cm × 1¾–8¾ cm). The leaf blade has five shallow or deeper sharp or blunt tipped [[Glossary of leaf morphology#palmately lobed|lobes that spread radially from a point]] with an entire margin.<ref name=JSAB>{{cite journal|last1= Olivier|first1= Maria C.|last2= van der Walt|first2= J.J.A.|year= 1984|title= The Taxonomy of the Pelargonium peltatum (L.) L'Hérit. Complex|journal= Journal of South African Botany|volume= 50|issue= 2|pages= 1–17}}</ref>

===Flowers===
The [[umbel]]-like [[inflorescence]]s sit atop a [[Peduncle (botany)|stalk]] of about 6½ cm (2.6 in) long (full range 4–8½ cm) covered with long soft hairs to hairless. At the top of the inflorescence stalk are long, softly hairy, oval to lance-shaped [[bract]]s of about 3 mm (0.12 in) long and 2 mm (0.08 in) wide, which subtend two to ten scentless flowers, each on a long softly hairy [[Pedicel (botany)|flower stalk]] of 1¾–5 mm (0.07–0.20 in) long. The long, softly hairy [[Hypanthium|floral tube]], which is somewhat difficult to distinguish from the flower stalk, is on average 3 cm (1.2 in) long (full range 2–4¼ cm). The five free, purple to light green [[sepal]]s are lance-shaped, covered in long, soft hairy on the surface facing out, on average 11 mm (0.44 in) long (full range 7½–14 mm). The five free [[petal]]s are spade-shaped, and whitish, pale pink, pinkish mauve or mauve in colour. 

The two upper petals sometimes have purple markings, curve back at an approximate angle of 90° and are on average 21 mm (0.85 in) long and 9 mm (0.35 in) wide (full range 15–27 mm × 6–12 mm). The three lower petals curve back slightly and are on average 17 mm (0.65 in) long and 6 mm (0.25 in) wide (full range 13½–21 mm × 3½–7½ mm). The ten [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|filaments]] are merged into a tube of about 2 mm (0.08 in) long, the free parts of the filaments varying in length within the same flower, between 2 and 11 mm (0.08–0.45 in) long. Only five to seven of the filaments carry a purple, about 2 mm long [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anther]], even in freshly opened flowers (anthers are quickly lost), the upper two on much shorter filaments. 

The woolly hairy [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] is about 4 mm (0.16 in) long that is topped by a hairy or hairless, about 5 mm (0.2 in) long [[Stigma (botany)#Style|style]] that carries five stigmas of about 3 mm (0.12 in) long. These [[Gynoecium|female floral parts]] develop into a [[Schizocarp|dry splitting fruit]], the five [[Mericarp|parts]] each consisting of an approximately 7 mm (0.28 in) long, roughly hairy oval base and an about 3 cm (1.2 in) long tail. The bases of these mericarps each contain one hairless, brown, ellipse-shaped [[seed]] of about 5 mm long and 2 mm in diameter.<ref name=JSAB /><ref>{{cite web|website= The Pelargonium Page|title= Ciconium (Sweet) Harv..|url= http://www.pelargonium.si/ciconium.html}}</ref>

''P. peltatum'' has nine [[Homologous chromosome|homologous sets of chromosomes]] (2x=18).<ref name=Bakker>{{cite journal|first1= Freek T.|last1= Bakker|first2= Alastair|last2= Culham|first3= Priyani|last3= Hettiarachi|first4= Tasoula|last4= Touloumenidou|first5= Mary|last5= Gibb|year= 2004|title= Phylogeny of Pelargonium (Geraniaceae) based on DNA Sequences from Three Genomes|journal= Taxon|volume= 53|issue= 1|pages= 17–28|doi= 10.2307/4135669|jstor= 4135669|url= https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/29285473.pdf}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
[[Image:Jan Moninckx08.jpg|upright=1.35|thumb|An aquarel depicting ''Pelargonium peltatum'', made in 1701 by [[Jan Moninckx]]]]The ivy-leaved pelargonium was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]], based on a specimen that was growing in the garden of [[George Clifford III]], in his 1753 groundbreaking book ''[[Species Plantarum]]'', and he named it ''Geranium peltatum''. When [[Charles Louis L'Héritier de Brutelle]] erected a new genus, ''Pelargonium'', in [[William Aiton]]’s book ''[[Hortus Kewensis]]'', published in 1789, he reassigned the species and made the [[new combination]] ''P. peltatum''. Later, in 1792, L'Héritier also described a comparable form and named it ''Pelargonium lateripes''. In 1796, the English botanist [[Richard Anthony Salisbury]] renamed ''P. lateripes'' to ''P. hederaefolium'', which is therefore a [[superfluous name]]. [[Henry Cranke Andrews]] in the first volume of his monography of the genus ''Geranium'', that was published in 1805, distinguished ''P. peltatum'' var. ''variegatum'', as well as ''G. hederinum''  var. ''flore albo'' and  var. ''variegatum''. In volume 2 that came out in 1806, he added ''P. peltatum'' var. ''superbum'' and ''G. hederinum''  var. ''zonales''. In his study ''Geraniaceae'', [[Robert Sweet (botanist)|Robert Sweet]], described two forms that he called ''P. scutellatum'' and ''P. pinquifolium'', although he suggested the latter may have been a [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]]. In 1824, [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] in his [[magnum opus]] ''[[Prodromus Systematis Naturalis Regni Vegetabilis]]'' described ''P. lateripes'' var. ''albomarginatum'' and var. ''walneri'', as well as ''P. peltatum'' var. ''zonatum''. In the same year, [[Johann Centurius Hoffmannsegg]] made a description of ''P. glabrum''. Sweet described in 1826 three more forms in his ''Hortus Brittanicus'', which he named ''P. lateripes'' var. ''roseus'', var. ''viridifolium'' and var. ''zonation''<!---sic--->. In 1835, [[Christian Friedrich Ecklon]] and [[Karl Ludwig Philipp Zeyher]] created a new genus, ''Dibrachya'', which they had based on the section that Sweet had erected earlier, and made the new combinations ''D. peltata'', ''D. scutellata'' and ''D. clypeata''. [[Ernst Gottlieb von Steudel]] moved the latter to ''Pelargonium'' creating ''P. clypeatum''. [[William Henry Harvey]] in the 1860 ''Flora Capensis'' made the new combinations ''P. peltatum'' var. ''scutellatum'', var. ''clypeatum'' and var. ''glabrum''. [[Jean Baptiste Saint-Lager]] changed the name of ''P. lateripes'' to ''P. lateripedatum'', a superfluous name in 1880. In 1890, [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1842)|Robert Brown (R.Br.ter)]] described ''P. saxifragoides''. [[Otto Kuntze]] erected the genus ''Geraniospermum'' and made the new combination ''Geraniospermum peltatum'' in 1891. As part of his extensive 1912 treatment of several plant families, [[Reinhard Gustav Paul Knuth]] described a form from [[Pondoland]] as ''P. bachmannii''.<ref name=JSAB /> 

Maria Olivier and [[J.J.A. van der Walt]] in 1984 considered the ivy-leaved pelargonium a pluriform species which includes plants that differ in the degree of succulence of the stems and leaves, the shape (circular or heart-shaped), the deepness of the incisions between the lobes, and the presence of a differently colored band in the leafblade. They conclude that several names correspond to garden hybrids, i.e. ''P. hederinum'' and its varieties ''flore albo'', ''variegatum'' and  ''zonale'', ''P. lateripes'' var. ''roseum'', ''viridiflorum'' and ''zonation'', ''P. peltatum'' var. ''superbum'' and var.  ''variegatum'', ''P. saxifragoides'' and finally ''P. pinquifolium''. The identity of  ''P. glabrum'' and ''P. bachmannii'' could not be determined because a [[Type (biology)|type]] could not be identified. The remaining forms all grade into each other, so these cannot be upheld as separate [[Taxon|taxa]] and are all [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] of ''P. peltatum''.<ref name=JSAB />

''Pelargonium peltatum'' has been assigned to the [[Section (biology)#In biology)|section]] ''Ciconium''.<ref>{{cite web|website= The Pelargonium Page|title= Pelargonium peltatum (L.) L'Hérit..|url= http://www.pelargonium.si/ciconium/peltatum.html}}</ref> A study comparing homologous [[DNA]] indicates that the members of a group consisting of ''[[Pelargonium acraeum|P. acraeum]]'', ''[[Pelargonium ranunculophyllum|P. ranunculophyllum]]'', ''[[Pelargonium alchemilloides|P. alchemilloides]]'', ''[[Pelargonium multibracteatum|P. multibracteatum]]'', ''[[Pelargonium tongaense|P. tongaense]]'', ''[[Pelargonium barklyi|P. barklyi]]'', ''[[Pelargonium articulatum|P. articulatum]]'', ''[[Pelargonium frutetorum|P. frutetorum]]'', ''[[Pelargonium inquinans|P. inquinans]]'', ''[[Pelargonium acetosum|P. acetosum]]'', ''[[Pelargonium zonale|P. zonale]]'', ''[[Pelargonium aridum|P. aridum]]'', ''[[Pelargonium socotrana|"P. socotrana"]]'', ''[[Pelargonium quinquelobatum|P. quinquelobatum]]''  and ''P. peltatum'' are most closely related.<ref name=Bakker />

The scientific name of the species ''peltatum'' is derived from the [[Latin]] word ''pelta'', a small crescent-shaped shield, and means "shield-bearing", a reference to the shield-like leaves, since the leaf stalk is attached to the centre of the leaf blade. The common name in [[Afrikaans]] is "kolsuring" (meaning cabbage sorrel) and refers to acid sap of the plant.<ref name=PZA />

== Distribution, habitat and ecology ==
The ivy-leaved pelargonium natural distribution consists of parts of the [[Western Cape]], [[Eastern Cape]], [[Kwazulu-Natal]] and [[Mpumalanga]] provinces of South Africa.<ref name=JSAB /> The species has [[escaped plant|escaped cultivation]] in climates somewhat comparable to South Africa including in California, Mexico, [[Puerto Rico]], [[Honduras]], [[Ecuador]] and the [[Galapagos Islands]], [[Spain]] and the [[Canary Islands]], [[Portugal]] and the [[Azores|Azores Islands]], [[France]], [[Italy]] and [[Greece]]. It may behave rather weedy.<ref name=CABI />

In the wild, it clambers over shrubs on dry rocky hillsides or along the coast on well-drained soils.<ref name=CABI />

The caterpillars of the [[common geranium bronze]] (''Cacyreus marshalli''), of [[Cacyreus dicksoni|Dickson's geranium bronze]] (''C. dicksoni''), and of the [[Cacyreus tespis|water bronze]] (''C. tespis'') eat the stems of pelargonium species. [[Carpenter bee]]s may be important pollinators as these frequent the flowers.<ref name=PZA />

== Conservation ==
The ivy-leaved pelargonium is considered a [[Least-concern species|species of least concern]] because of its large distribution and stable population.<ref>{{cite web|website= SANBI Red List of South African Plants|title= Kolsuring|url= http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=1976-253}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
In 1700, [[Willem Adriaan van der Stel]], Governor of the [[Cape Colony]], introduced the ivy-leaved pelargonium to the Netherlands.<ref name=PZA /> Sir [[Francis Masson]] shipped the species to Great Britain in 1774. ''P. peltatum'' has been used to develop many garden hybrids that are called "[[Pelargonium#B. Ivy-leaved pelargoniums (derived from Pelargonium peltatum)|ivy-leaved pelargoniums]]". The species and its hybrids can be very easily propagated through taking cuttings.<ref name=PZA /> It grows best on well drained substrates such as sandy or loamy soils, is not sensitive to soil acidity and is drought resistant, but it neither tolerates shading nor frost. The ivy-leaved pelargonium is cultivated on a large-scale for landscaping and as an ornamental plant for use in gardens and containers, as well as being used as a [[houseplant]].<ref name=CABI />

== Uses ==
The leaves of the ivy-leaved pelargonium can be eaten as a vegetable and have a [[Taste#Sourness|tangy]] taste. A bluish textile dye can be made from the petals.<ref>{{cite web|website= Plants for a Future|title= Pelargonium peltatum – (L.)L'Hér..|url= https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Pelargonium+peltatum}}</ref>
